input: The nurse records diabetes treatment, the disputed loss-of-awareness history and the visual symptoms as separate issues needing clarification, without automatically classifying the event as a diabetic complication.

The driver describes a short period of unresponsiveness after a delayed lunch and believes it was a low glucose episode because he uses insulin, but the witness says his hand twitched before he stopped speaking and cannot remember whether he answered immediately after a sweet drink.
No glucose was measured until approximately 25 minutes later, when it was 4.8 mmol/L, and the nurse has no contemporaneous clinical record confirming hypoglycaemia, a seizure or another cause.

An emergency note lists possible cardiac syncope and requests further investigation, whereas the driver's own description calls the event a faint; neither document records a firm mechanism or an assessment of recurrence risk.

His blood-pressure medicines were changed after BP 180/106 mmHg at a pharmacy last week, whereas today's BP 152/90 mmHg was measured only once; he reports occasional dizziness but no definite loss of consciousness.

The driver says his hearing is adequate when both aids are working, although radio instructions become difficult after several hours and he sometimes removes the left aid because of discomfort; his supervisor reports missed instructions, while the driver attributes these to a damaged radio speaker.

An unsigned worksheet states unaided better ear average 39 dB averaged over 0.5, 1, 2 and 3 kHz, but the driver remembers wearing at least one aid during testing and cannot confirm that the sheet belongs to the most recent appointment.

The same folder contains an earlier note stating bilateral hearing loss and another form marked Hearing: normal, with no explanation of whether the statements refer to aided performance or unaided testing.
